implementation_notes: Go folds the guard into the language: a receive from an empty channel blocks until a sender arrives, a send on an unbuffered channel blocks until a receiver is ready, and close(ch) is a broadcast (the official sync.Cond documentation states that for many simple cases channels are the better tool, with close corresponding to Broadcast and send to Signal). So the guarded suspension of 'wait until work is available' is a plain channel operation, and buffered channels supply the 'space available' half of a bounded handoff. sync.Cond remains for guards that read compound state which must be mutated under a mutex, and select with a timer or context supplies the bounded wait that a bare receive lacks.
pitfalls: A nil channel blocks forever and a closed channel never blocks: both are silent hangs or busy loops where a guard was intended.
Sending on a closed channel panics, so close is only safe as the broadcast case when all senders are done.
A bare receive has no timeout: use select with time.After or a context deadline for any wait on a request path.

variants.name: sync.Mutex + sync.Cond (explicit predicate wait)
variants.implementation_notes: sync.Cond is the explicit form: Wait atomically unlocks its Locker and suspends the goroutine, and its source documentation insists the caller waits in a loop because the condition may still be false on return; Signal wakes one waiter, Broadcast all of them, and the signaller need not hold the lock. Choose it over channels when several predicates share one lock or when every waiter must re-evaluate a compound condition under the mutex, and remember that a Cond arranges a happens-before edge from Broadcast/Signal to the Wait it unblocks.
pitfalls: A Cond must not be copied after first use; the runtime detects copies and panics, so keep it behind a pointer inside the guarded object.
Signal only wakes a goroutine that is already waiting, which is why the predicate must be written under the same mutex and re-checked in a loop.
